first_impression.reaction: My assistant shortlisted it and summarised it first. The opening answers the question in one line and doesn't gush: 'In most cases, yes: an overseas marriage is generally recognised here if it was valid where it took place and would have been valid under Australian law.' Fine. It reads like something a lawyer wouldn't wince at, and there's no talk of being 'affordable', so the brand doesn't lose me on the first screen. But it's a paperwork guide written for a couple who live in Australia. We live in Dubai. I read the takeaways, the symbolic ceremony section and the close myself. The rest goes to whoever handles our legal side.

journey.quote: The harder questions start once you are home: you cannot register the marriage here, the certificate is in Italian, and a surname change is a separate application in several states.
journey.reaction: Clear and honest about where the friction is. I'd rather know that now than find out when a bank refuses a document.

journey.section: When an Italian marriage would not be recognised
journey.quote: one of you was domiciled in Australia and either of you was under marriageable age
journey.reaction: The whole page assumes we're domiciled in Australia. We're not. Our family is in Sydney and London, we live in Dubai. Does any of this change for us? The page never says.

journey.section: Make sure it is registered in Italy
journey.quote: Before you leave Italy, ask for the comune's certificate, not the parish's.
journey.reaction: A precise, practical instruction. This is the kind of detail that tells me someone has actually done this before.

journey.quote: Not published: Prefettura processing times. Ask your Wedded Advisor to build the appointment into your plan.
journey.reaction: Good. I don't want to know how to book a Prefettura appointment. I want someone else to have it in the run sheet. Honest that the timing isn't published, too.

journey.section: Marry legally in Australia first, celebrate in Italy
journey.quote: You can sidestep most of this by signing the legal papers at home and keeping the Italian day for the vows, the dinner and the people.
journey.reaction: This is the route that actually interests me, because it keeps the Italian day about the guests and not about a registrar. But 'at home' for us isn't Australia. Can we do the legal part in Sydney when we're there, or in Dubai or London? The page only explains the Australian notice.

journey.section: The trade-offs if Italy should be 'the' wedding
journey.quote: The cost is emotional. Your legal anniversary becomes a short ceremony at home, and some couples feel the Italian vows repeat something already done.
journey.reaction: Understated, and true. I appreciate that it doesn't pretend there's no trade-off.

journey.quote: Can you divorce in Australia if you married in Italy?
journey.reaction: Our family office will care more about what happens to property and agreements under Italian law than about divorce eligibility. That is the legal question a family like ours actually asks, and it isn't here.

journey.section: Get the legal side settled before you book
journey.quote: Your Wedded Advisor is one person from first idea to the last dance, working in your time zone and quoting in AUD, and confirms in writing what is included before you commit.
journey.reaction: One person, my time zone: good. 'Quoting in AUD' and 'what is included' make it sound like I'm buying a package off a list. I'm not interested in what's included. I'm interested in what's possible.

unanswered_questions: We live in Dubai, not Australia. Does domicile change whether an Italian marriage is recognised for us, and which Australian rules still apply?
If we marry legally first and keep Italy symbolic, can the legal ceremony be in Dubai or London rather than Australia, and would Australia recognise that?
Can the civil ceremony happen privately at our own venue, or does it have to be at the town hall? Are our names posted publicly anywhere in Italy beforehand?
What does marrying in Italy mean for property and any prenuptial agreement? Will you work with our family lawyers on that?
If our family also wants its own religious ceremony that isn't Catholic, how does that sit alongside the Italian civil marriage?
Who physically handles the certificate, apostille and translation for us, so we don't have to queue at a Prefettura the week after the wedding?
Has this team handled the legal side for a wedding of 200 to 400 guests with VIPs, where discretion matters?

turn_offs_found.quote: Your Wedded Advisor is one person from first idea to the last dance, working in your time zone and quoting in AUD, and confirms in writing what is included before you commit.
turn_offs_found.why: 'What is included' is package language. It makes me feel like a standard client choosing from a menu.

would_share_with: My assistant, to file for the family office's lawyers
My mother in Sydney, for the 'marry legally first' section

cta_reaction.quote: When you are ready, [speak with a Wedded Advisor](https://weddedwonderland.com/wonderland-concierge) about which route suits you.
cta_reaction.why: My assistant might click to see what the concierge page looks like. I wouldn't fill in a general form myself. I'd want a private introduction, or a direct line to someone senior, and some sign you've done weddings at our scale. Nothing on this page tells me that, though I accept it's a legal guide.

top_3_changes: Add one short line for couples who live outside Australia (domicile, and where the legal ceremony can happen if Italy is symbolic), or say plainly that their Wedded Advisor confirms this for their situation.

Rewrite the close so it isn't package language: drop 'what is included' and 'quoting in AUD' in favour of the advisor handling the certificate, apostille and translation for you, working alongside your own lawyers, with a private conversation as the next step.
If it can be sourced, say whether the Italian civil ceremony can be held privately at the venue and whether anything is posted publicly beforehand. Discretion is the first thing I'd ask.
